reference.source: Williams Obstetrics / RCOG guidance on cervical cerclage and preterm birth prevention
clinicalPearls: Cervical insufficiency is painless cervical dilatation and shortening leading to mid-trimester pregnancy loss or preterm birth without overt contractions
The classic history is recurrent second-trimester losses with painless dilatation, sometimes with bulging membranes
Risk factors include previous cervical surgery or trauma, prior mechanical dilatation, and congenital connective tissue or uterine anomalies
Serial transvaginal ultrasound measurement of cervical length in at-risk women helps identify progressive shortening
Management options include cervical cerclage, vaginal progesterone, and a cervical pessary depending on history and findings
Cerclage may be offered on the basis of obstetric history, ultrasound-detected shortening, or as a rescue procedure for premature dilatation
It must be distinguished from preterm labour and from infection or abruption, which change management
Excluding infection and ruptured membranes is essential before intervention such as rescue cerclage
reference.pathophysiology: Cervical insufficiency reflects structural or functional weakness of the cervix so that it cannot retain the pregnancy against the increasing mechanical load of the growing uterus. Deficient cervical stroma, whether from congenital collagen abnormality or acquired damage after surgery or trauma, leads to progressive painless shortening, funnelling, and dilatation, often in the second trimester. As the cervix opens, membranes may prolapse and become exposed to the vaginal flora, predisposing to rupture, ascending infection, and subsequent loss or preterm delivery. In practice a spectrum exists, with inflammation and subclinical infection frequently interacting with mechanical weakness.
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound cervical length measurement, with serial monitoring in at-risk women
Speculum examination to assess dilatation and detect membranes or fluid
Tests for ruptured membranes when suspected
Screening for genital and urinary infection
Assessment of uterine anatomy in recurrent loss
Foetal wellbeing and viability assessment on ultrasound
redFlags: Painless cervical dilatation with bulging or exposed membranes
Signs of intra-amniotic infection such as fever, tenderness, or offensive discharge
Rapidly progressing dilatation in the mid-trimester
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause, gestation, and timeliness of intervention. History-indicated and ultrasound-indicated cerclage can improve outcomes in appropriately selected women, whereas advanced dilatation with prolapsing membranes or infection carries a high risk of loss or extreme preterm birth.
pitfalls: Placing a cerclage without excluding infection or ruptured membranes
Labelling a first mid-trimester loss as insufficiency without considering other causes
Missing coexisting preterm labour or abruption and delaying appropriate care
Failing to monitor cervical length in women with relevant risk factors
references: National guidance on prevention of preterm birth
management: Offer cervical cerclage indicated by obstetric history, ultrasound-detected shortening, or as a rescue procedure for premature dilatation
Prescribe vaginal progesterone to lower preterm birth risk in women with a short cervix
Consider a cervical pessary as an alternative or adjunct in selected women
Undertake serial transvaginal ultrasound cervical length monitoring in at-risk pregnancies
Screen for and treat genital and urinary infection and assess for ruptured membranes
Give antenatal corticosteroids for foetal lung maturity and magnesium sulphate for neuroprotection if preterm birth is imminent
Refer to maternal-foetal medicine and provide pre-conception counselling for future pregnancies
